title: Why Carboxylic Acids Boil So High: Hydrogen-Bonded Dimers
subject: Chemistry
objective: Four molecules of about the same mass boil from 0 °C to 118 °C. Carboxylic acids win because two hydrogen bonds join them into dimers that survive even in the vapour; the same dimers double acetic acid's measured molar mass in benzene.

fill.q: Two acetic acid molecules held by two hydrogen bonds form a ____.
Acetic acid's molar mass measured in benzene is about ____.
Aliphatic acids are miscible with water up to ____ carbons.

tf.q: Carboxylic acids boil higher than alcohols of similar molar mass.
Hydrogen bonds in carboxylic acids are completely broken in the vapour phase.
tf.explain: Most acids remain dimers in the vapour.

tf.q: Benzoic acid dissolves readily in cold water.
tf.explain: It is nearly insoluble in cold water.

ar.a: Acetic acid shows an abnormal molar mass in benzene.
Hexanoic acid is less soluble in water than ethanoic acid.
ar.r: Its larger hydrocarbon part does not hydrogen-bond with water.

mcq.q: In the dimer, the hydrogen of O–H bonds to:
options: the C=O oxygen of the other molecule

num.q: How many hydrogen bonds hold one carboxylic acid dimer together?

short.q: Draw the acetic acid dimer and explain why acetic acid boils at 118 °C while propan-1-ol boils at 97 °C.
short.solution: Two CH₃COOH molecules joined by two O–H···O=C hydrogen bonds; this stronger, more extensive association (persisting even in the vapour) needs more energy to overcome than the single H-bonds of the alcohol.

match.explain: Each compound matches its boiling point.
